# Introduction: CAD, Construction, and Carpentry {.unnumbered}

Before you draw a post or extrude a rail, it helps to know what kind of tool
you are holding. CAD has a short but dense history, and the choices made along
the way still shape what a modeler is good at—and what it quietly ignores.

This introduction is a map, not a complete history. It covers where CAD came
from, how construction and carpentry adopted it, the main trade-offs you face
when choosing a tool, and where SolidCraft sits among them.

## From numerical control to Sketchpad

CAD did not begin as a way to make prettier drawings. It began as a way to
control machines and to make engineering drawings that could be changed without
redrawing every line.

In the 1950s, numerical control (NC) and the APT programming language separated
the geometry of a part from the hand movements of a machinist. A toolpath could
be described, stored, and replayed. That idea—geometry as data—is the root of
everything that follows.

In 1963, Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad at MIT showed a different possibility:
a person drawing directly on a screen with a light pen, with constraints and
reusable symbols. Sketchpad is often called the first interactive CAD program.
Its important idea was not the pen. It was that a drawing could be a model with
rules, not ink on a page.

Around the same time, General Motors and IBM developed DAC-1 (Design Augmented
by Computers), one of the first interactive design systems, used on car bodies. The two strands—machine control and interactive design—were
already pointing toward the modern CAD model: geometry that can be computed,
checked, and used to make something.

## The turnkey years

Through the 1970s, CAD lived on expensive minicomputers sold as turnkey
systems by companies such as Computervision, Calma, and Applicon. Drafters used
them for 2D drawings, layers, blocks, dimensions, and repeated details. The
work was faster and more consistent than a drawing board, but the hardware and
software were out of reach for a small carpentry shop.

The 1980s changed that. AutoCAD arrived in 1982 and put 2D drafting on
personal computers. At the same time, solid modeling research matured into
commercial tools. Boundary representation (B-rep) and constructive solid
geometry (CSG) made it possible to compute volumes, intersections, and
manufacturable shapes rather than only draw their projections.

In 1988, Pro/ENGINEER popularized a different way of working: parametric,
feature-based, history-based modeling. Dimensions became drivers. A part was a
sequence of features, and changing an early dimension rebuilt the later ones.
That is the model most modern mechanical CAD still uses, and it is the model
this book uses for carpentry.

## Solids, assemblies, and buildings

The 1990s brought parametric modeling to the desktop. SolidWorks (1995) made
history-based solid modeling more affordable and more approachable. In
construction, a parallel shift was happening under the name BIM—building
information modeling. A building was no longer only a set of lines; it was a
database of walls, slabs, openings, materials, and relationships. Revit, which
arrived in 2000, became one of the best-known expressions of that idea.

BIM is powerful for large projects because it coordinates many trades,
detects clashes, and produces quantities from the same model. It is also a
different kind of tool from a part modeler. A BIM authoring system expects
walls, levels, families, and a whole building. A carpentry part modeler expects
a board, a joint, and a cut list.

The 2000s and 2010s added cloud collaboration, browser-based CAD, direct
modeling (editing geometry without a long history), and much closer links to
digital fabrication. CNC routers, beam saws, panel optimizers, and timber
framing machines consume geometry directly. A model can now become a cut file,
a drilling pattern, or a machine path.

In the 2020s, the newest layer is programmability. CAD tools expose APIs and
scripts; AI agents can call those APIs through protocols such as MCP. The
interesting question is no longer only "can the tool draw it?" but "can the
tool explain, repeat, and verify what it drew?"

| Period | What changed | Why it mattered |
|--------|--------------|-----------------|
| 1950s–1960s | NC, APT, Sketchpad, DAC-1 | Geometry became programmable and interactive |
| 1970s | Turnkey 2D drafting | Drawings became digital, but stayed expensive |
| 1980s | PCs, AutoCAD, commercial solid modeling | CAD reached small firms; solids became computable |
| 1990s–2000s | Parametric feature modeling, BIM | Design intent and building data became central |
| 2000s–2010s | Cloud CAD, direct modeling, digital fabrication | Collaboration and machine-ready geometry |
| 2020s | APIs, scripts, AI agents, MCP | Models can be automated, inspected, and delegated |

## CAD on the job site

Construction adopted CAD in layers.

**First as drawings.** Plans, elevations, sections, details, and shop drawings
replaced or supplemented hand drafting. Layers and blocks made repeated details
consistent. Much of the industry still runs on 2D PDFs, and that is not a
failure; a clear plan sheet is still one of the best communication devices ever
invented.

**Then as a coordination model.** BIM brought geometry, properties, and
relationships together. On large projects, the model can detect a duct passing
through a beam before anyone orders steel. It can also produce schedules and
quantities that would take days to count by hand.

**Then as a fabrication input.** CNC routers, panel saws, and timber processing
machines cut from digital geometry. Cabinet shops nest parts on sheets; timber
framers cut joinery from a model; deck and fence shops pre-cut kits. The model
becomes a set of instructions, not just a picture.

For a small carpentry project, the most useful unit is usually not a whole
building. It is a part or a small assembly: a fence panel, a gate, a deck frame,
a stair, a shed wall. That is the scale where a parametric solid model pays for
itself quickly. You can check a spacing, count the boards, and see the joint
before you cut.

What CAD does not do is equally important. It does not measure the site for
you. It does not know that the lumber is wet, cupped, or 3 mm under size. It
does not grant a permit or prove a beam is strong enough. Those remain
judgement, measurement, and code work.

## The main choices

There is no single best CAD tool. The choice follows the project, the shop, and
the people who have to use the output.

| Decision | Options | Carpentry consequence |
|----------|---------|-----------------------|
| Scope | 2D drafting, 3D solids, BIM | A plan sheet is fast; a solid answers fit and volume; BIM coordinates a whole building |
| Editing | Direct, parametric history | Direct is quick for exploration; parametric preserves intent and rebuilds |
| Geometry | Solid, surface, mesh | Solids are right for boards and joints; meshes are for visualization and printing |
| Location | Desktop, browser, cloud | Local is private and offline; cloud is easier to share but depends on a service |
| License | Proprietary, open source | Commercial brings ecosystem and support; open source brings cost, control, and inspectability |
| Focus | General CAD, BIM, trade-specific | General CAD is flexible; trade tools bring libraries and production rules |
| Control | Manual, scripts, agents | Automation is faster and repeatable, but requires a review loop |

The last row is the one this book cares about most. A model that can be
scripted is also a model that can be checked, repeated, and explained. That is
useful even if you never ask an AI to touch it.

## Where SolidCraft fits

SolidCraft is an open-source parametric solid modeler. It is not a BIM
authoring tool, and it does not try to be one. It works at the scale of parts
and small assemblies, which is exactly the scale of a fence, a deck, or a shed.

A few things make it unusual:

- **It is open source** under MIT or Apache-2.0. You can inspect it, run it
  locally, and keep your designs in ordinary files.
- **It runs in several places**—desktop app, browser app, headless CLI, and an
  MCP server—with the same command set underneath.
- **Everything is a command.** The toolbar, the command palette, a script, the
  CLI, and an AI agent all run the same JSON commands. A simple design can be
  replayed from a script, which makes it reproducible and teachable; designs
  with components or joints are still a scripting limitation.
- **It is parametric.** Sketches have constraints and dimensions; features sit
  on a timeline; changing a parameter rebuilds the model.
- **It speaks useful formats.** STEP and IGES import and export, plus 3MF, STL,
  OBJ, and glTF where supported. For carpentry, STEP is the useful neutral
  exchange format; meshes are for visualization, not measurement.
- **It does not require a high-end workstation.** A current GPU with Vulkan,
  Direct3D 12, Metal, or OpenGL is best; a software renderer is a slow fallback.
  The headless CLI can build and measure without a window.

The combination is rare: open source, local-first, parametric, and
command-driven, with the same model reachable from a person, a script, and an
agent. For a learning book, that transparency matters more than a long feature
list. You can see what the tool did, replay it, and change one variable at a
time.

::: {.callout-warning}
SolidCraft is early. Surfaces, construction drawings, CAM, and simulation are
deferred, and the feature set is smaller than a mature commercial CAD or BIM
package. It is excellent for learning the geometry of carpentry parts and small
assemblies; it is not a substitute for a structural engineer, a building
department, or a shop's established production pipeline.
:::

## Two tools, two jobs

This book uses SolidCraft and FreeCAD together, not as interchangeable
alternatives but as two tools with different strengths.

- **SolidCraft** is the fast part modeler: sketch, extrude, check, repeat, and
  drive it with a small native command set. It owns the SolidCraft track
  (Parts I–III).
- **FreeCAD** is the broader platform: Part Design, Spreadsheets, TechDraw
  drawings, BIM with IFC, and a mature Python API. It owns the FreeCAD track
  (Part IV).

The overlap is real. Both sketch, constrain, extrude, and parameterize. The
split is about deliverables. If you need a part, a figure, and a cut list,
SolidCraft is quicker. If you need a dimensioned shop drawing, an IFC model, or
a Python-driven workflow, FreeCAD is the better owner.

For a side-by-side comparison with the main open-source BIM tools, including
Bonsai, see [Appendix D](../appendices/d-open-source-landscape.qmd).

## How this book uses them

The SolidCraft track stays at the part-and-assembly scale. You model posts,
rails, pickets, joists, decking, studs, and a simple roof, then turn those
models into figures and a bill of materials. The FreeCAD track rebuilds the same
projects, adds TechDraw sheets, and turns the shed into a small BIM model with
IFC export.

You will not model a whole house, a full set of construction documents, or a
machine-ready production line. The conventions are simple: millimetres, Z up,
actual lumber dimensions, a datum you can find on site, and a check for every
model. The goal is not to memorize buttons. It is to build enough judgement that
you can look at a model and know which dimensions matter, which clearances are
missing, and which questions belong on site rather than on screen.

## Further reading

- Ivan Sutherland, *Sketchpad: A Man-Machine Graphical Communication System*
  (1963), available as a Cambridge technical report:
  <https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-574.pdf>
- SolidCraft documentation: <https://docs.solidcraft.io/>
- FreeCAD documentation: <https://wiki.freecad.org>
- FreeCAD MCP: <https://github.com/neka-nat/freecad-mcp>
- Charles Eastman, Paul Teicholz, Rafael Sacks, and Ghang Lee, *BIM Handbook:
  A Guide to Building Information Modeling for Owners, Designers, Engineers,
  Contractors, and Facility Managers*, 3rd edition (Wiley, 2018).

Dates in this introduction are approximate, and the history is selective. The
aim is to explain why today's tools look the way they do, not to settle
priority claims about individual inventions.
